paragraphs.context: Words have always swirled around me like snowflakes—each
paragraphs.simple: Melody says words fall around her like snowflakes. Each one is special, but she can never hold on to them.

paragraphs.context: From the time I was really little—maybe just a few months old—words were like sweet, liquid gifts, and I
paragraphs.simple: Since she was a baby, Melody has loved words. Her parents talked, sang and whispered to her all the time, and she took in every word.

paragraphs.context: I have no idea how I untangled the complicated process of words and thought, but it happened quickly and naturally. By
paragraphs.simple: No one knows how, but by age two Melody understood words and could think in them.

paragraphs.context: I have never spoken one single word. I am almost eleven years old.
paragraphs.simple: The big surprise: Melody is almost eleven, and she has never said a single word out loud.

paragraphs.context: I can’t talk. I can’t walk. I can’t feed
paragraphs.simple: Melody cannot talk, walk, eat by herself or go to the bathroom alone. She jokes about it with "Big bummer."

paragraphs.context: My arms and hands are pretty stiff, but I
paragraphs.simple: Her arms and hands are stiff. She can push buttons on a remote and move her wheelchair, but she cannot hold a spoon or a pencil.

paragraphs.context: When people look at me, I guess they see
paragraphs.simple: Melody imagines how strangers see her: a small girl strapped into a pink wheelchair. She says the pink color does not make it nicer.

paragraphs.context: Her body tends to move on its own agenda
paragraphs.mainIdea: A body with its own plan.
paragraphs.simple: Melody's arms and legs sometimes move by themselves and knock things over. She cannot control them.

paragraphs.context: And music. Songs floated through me and stayed. Lullabies
paragraphs.simple: Music stays inside Melody. When she hears music she "sees" colors and "smells" pictures.

background.note: Some people really feel two senses at once: for example, they see a color when they hear a sound. This is called synesthesia. Melody describes music this way all through the book.

paragraphs.context: Dad is partial to jazz, and every chance he
paragraphs.simple: Dad loves jazz and plays it to annoy Mom, who loves classical music. To Melody, jazz is brown and smells like wet dirt.

paragraphs.context: How did I already know the words and the
paragraphs.simple: Melody heard a song on the radio and somehow knew it. She got so excited that she shook and pointed, but Mom did not understand.

paragraphs.context: How could she understand that I loved the song
paragraphs.simple: The song was "Elvira" by the Oak Ridge Boys. Melody cannot explain to Mom that country music makes her smell lemons.

background.note: A popular American country song from 1981 by the Oak Ridge Boys. Later Melody names her talking machine "Elvira" after it.

paragraphs.context: I suppose it’s a good thing to be unable
paragraphs.simple: Melody remembers everything. That is good, but it also frustrates her, because she cannot share any of it.

paragraphs.context: Mostly, though, I remember words. Very early I figured
paragraphs.simple: Melody understood early that the world is full of words, and that everyone around her can say them easily. She cannot.

paragraphs.context: I guess I figured out I was different a
paragraphs.simple: Slowly Melody saw that her mind worked well but her body did not. This surprised her and made her angry.

paragraphs.context: Even though he sometimes made up his own vocabulary
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dad talks to her like a grown-up.
paragraphs.simple: Dad never used baby talk. He spoke to Melody with real words, sure that she understood. He was right.

paragraphs.context: “Your life is not going to be easy, little
paragraphs.simple: Dad tells Melody her life will be hard. He says he would gladly change places with her if he could.

paragraphs.context: When he could, Dad read to me. Even though
paragraphs.simple: Even when he was tired, Dad read picture books to Melody. She remembers every word of them.

background.note: Famous American picture books for young children, by Maurice Sendak and Dr. Seuss.

paragraphs.context: Here’s the thing: I’m ridiculously smart, and I’m pretty
paragraphs.simple: Melody says she is very smart. She remembers everything she sees or hears, like a camera taking pictures.

paragraphs.context: Not that it does me a lot of good
paragraphs.simple: All this knowledge is locked inside Melody. Only Mom has a feeling that Melody understands things.

paragraphs.context: So every once in a while I really lose
paragraphs.simple: Sometimes Melody's body goes wild: her arms and legs lash out and she screams. She says these are not seizures.

paragraphs.context: These things—I call them my “tornado explosions”— are
paragraphs.simple: Melody calls these fits "tornado explosions". All her frustration bursts out, and she cannot stop it.

paragraphs.context: Then, in the toy section, I saw them. Brightly
paragraphs.simple: In a big store, Melody saw toy blocks that TV news said were dangerous because of lead paint.

background.note: Lead is a metal that can poison children. When a toy is found to have lead paint, the company "recalls" it: it asks stores to stop selling it and buyers to send it back.

paragraphs.context: I didn’t want the blocks. I wanted to tell
paragraphs.simple: Melody wanted to tell Mom the blocks were dangerous, but all she could do was scream and point.

paragraphs.context: Mom got to the door of the store, yanked
paragraphs.simple: Mom pulled Melody out of the store, leaving all her shopping behind. She was close to tears and asked what was wrong with her.

paragraphs.context: I’ve seen dozens of doctors in my life, who
paragraphs.simple: Doctors cannot help Melody and do not understand her. So she pretends she understands nothing, which is what they expect anyway.

paragraphs.context: When I turned five, it was time to think
paragraphs.simple: At age five, Mom took Melody to a doctor who tested how smart she was, to decide where she should go to school. If her seat belt opens, she slides out of the chair like a piece of wet spaghetti.

paragraphs.context: He brought out a stack of well-used, hopefully
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dr. Hugely talks down to her.
paragraphs.simple: The doctor speaks loudly and slowly, as if Melody cannot hear and is stupid. He asks her to stack blocks she cannot even hold.

paragraphs.context: But who was being stupid? Didn’t he know I
paragraphs.simple: Melody cannot pick up the blocks, so she knocks them all onto the floor. She thinks the doctor is the stupid one.

paragraphs.context: He showed me pictures of a tomato, a cherry
paragraphs.mainIdea: Too easy, so she picks another answer.
paragraphs.simple: The doctor wants her to choose the round red balloon. Melody picks the banana, because it is the only one that is not round and red.

paragraphs.context: Now, I watch Animal Planet all the time. I
paragraphs.simple: Melody knows that cows, whales, camels and elephants all have babies called calves, so she points to all four. The doctor thinks she is wrong.

paragraphs.context: I knew all the colors and shapes and animals
paragraphs.simple: Melody knows colors, shapes, numbers, Spanish words and hundreds of songs. But she cannot show anyone.

paragraphs.context: “It takes time to accept the limitations of a
paragraphs.simple: The doctor tells Mom the name of Melody's condition. He says Mom must learn to accept her child's limits.

background.note: A condition caused by damage to the brain before, during or soon after birth. It makes it hard to control muscles. Many people with CP, like Melody, are as smart as anyone else.

paragraphs.context: Dr. Hugely looked from her to me. He shook
paragraphs.simple: Dr. Hugely says Melody will never walk, talk, take care of herself or understand more than simple instructions.

paragraphs.context: “Let’s see,” the doctor said, “Melody is, ah, five
paragraphs.simple: The doctor suggests sending Melody to live in a special home, so her parents can "get on with their lives". Melody is scared.

paragraphs.context: Mom wasn’t looking at me. She was staring daggers
paragraphs.simple: Mom stands up and says they will never send Melody away. She throws the brochure in the trash.

paragraphs.context: Mom was on a roll. “You’re not so intelligent
paragraphs.mainIdea: "She's the one with the true intelligence!"
paragraphs.simple: Mom says the doctor is only lucky, not smart. Melody is clever because she manages in a world where nothing works for her.

paragraphs.context: Kids who, for the most part, ignore kids like
paragraphs.simple: After a long list of what normal kids do, Melody ends with the sad truth: most of them ignore kids like her.

paragraphs.context: When the weather is bright and sunny, we sit
paragraphs.simple: Melody watches the other kids play four-square. They never ask the kids in wheelchairs to join, and she wishes someone would.

paragraphs.context: I am in a special program with other children
paragraphs.mainIdea: A class that never moves up.
paragraphs.simple: Melody is in a special class for kids with disabilities. They do the same things every year with a new teacher, and never move on.

paragraphs.context: Our classroom, room H-5, might be nice for babies
paragraphs.simple: Room H-5 is painted with smiling suns, bunnies and puppies. Melody thinks it is made for babies, not ten-year-olds.

paragraphs.context: Every Christmas they make the kids in H-5 decorate
paragraphs.simple: Every Christmas the H-5 kids must decorate the same old Styrofoam snowman. Melody hates it.

paragraphs.context: “Do you like the snowman, Ashley?” Mrs. Hyatt asked
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ashley can only say yes or no.
paragraphs.simple: Ashley's body is so stiff that her board has only two words. She turns her head toward "no" when asked if she likes the snowman.

paragraphs.context: Even though she has trouble figuring out complicated stuff
paragraphs.simple: Maria has Down syndrome. She finds hard things difficult, but she always knows how people feel. She knew Melody was sad when her goldfish died.

paragraphs.context: If Maria is our hugger, Gloria is our rocker
paragraphs.simple: Gloria sits in a corner and rocks back and forth for hours. She seems to be autistic. She can walk, and she talks only when she has something to say.

paragraphs.context: When Sydney the Snowman comes out of whatever box
paragraphs.simple: Willy can't control his arms, so the teachers keep him away from the snowman. He has knocked it over many times.

paragraphs.context: Sometimes when I look at Willy, though, I get
paragraphs.simple: Melody thinks Willy wishes he could be quiet and calm. Sometimes he tries very hard, and for a few minutes he is.

paragraphs.context: I have a large Plexiglas tray that fastens to
paragraphs.simple: Melody's tray is also her communication board. It has only a small number of words on it, so she can say very little.

paragraphs.context: I like all the kids in room H-5, and
paragraphs.simple: Melody likes her classmates, but no one else is like her. She feels trapped, with no way to tell anyone how to free her.

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Violet Valencia lives next door to us. Violets
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Violet Valencia, Melody's neighbor, is a very tall woman with huge hands. Melody finds her as unusual as a "purple orange".

paragraphs.context: Mrs. V and Mom used to work together as
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V used to be a nurse with Mom. She wore bright clothes at the hospital because she believes color gives sick children hope.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, gag me!” Mrs. V said, startling him. “Don’t
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V tells Dad not to worry about soft words from books about disabled children. She is sure Melody can learn.

paragraphs.context: From the very beginning, Mrs. Valencia gave me no
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V put Melody on the floor on a quilt and left her there. Melody cried and screamed, but Mrs. V ignored her.

paragraphs.context: Then she came back and put my favorite toy
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V put Melody's favorite toy monkey just out of reach. Melody was lying on her back and could not get it.

paragraphs.context: So I did. I strained. I reached. I tried
paragraphs.simple: Melody tried so hard that she rolled onto her stomach for the first time. She was very proud.

paragraphs.context: Once I started school, however, I discovered I had
paragraphs.simple: At school Melody found a bigger problem: she could not talk, so she could not answer or ask questions.

paragraphs.context: Now I’m interested in almost anything that has a
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V shows Melody a TV program about Stephen Hawking, a famous scientist who cannot walk or talk but is very smart.

background.note: Stephen Hawking (1942-2018) was a British scientist who studied space and time. A disease called ALS took away his ability to move and speak, so he "talked" with a computer that made a voice.

paragraphs.context: So Mrs. V made it her new mission to
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V decided to give Melody language. She filled Melody's board with many small words, names and questions.

paragraphs.context: I have magic thumbs, by the way. They work
paragraphs.simple: Most of Melody's body does not work right, but her thumbs work perfectly. She uses them to point and press.

paragraphs.context: I learned big words, like caterpillar and mosquito, and
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V taught Melody to read hundreds of words with flash cards, from short rhymes to big words. Melody loved it.

paragraphs.context: She rolled me down the ramp Dad had built
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V let Melody sit in the warm summer rain until they were both soaking wet. Melody laughed and laughed.

paragraphs.context: When I sleep, I dream. And in my dreams
paragraphs.mainIdea: In her dreams she can do anything.
paragraphs.simple: In her dreams Melody runs, dances and talks with friends on the phone.

paragraphs.context: When I wake up in the morning, it’s always
paragraphs.simple: Every morning Melody is disappointed to wake up and remember her real life.

paragraphs.context: She figured out I liked books, so she got
paragraphs.simple: Her second-grade teacher, Mrs. Tracy, saw that Melody loved books and gave her audiobooks. When the books were too easy, Mrs. Tracy found harder ones.

paragraphs.context: I listened to all of the Baby-Sitters Club
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Tracy tested Melody after each book, and Melody answered every question correctly.

paragraphs.context: The next year it all unraveled. I know teachers
paragraphs.simple: In third grade everything fell apart. The new teacher, Mrs. Billups, did not know what Melody could do.

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Billups started every morning by playing her favorite
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Billups played silly songs for little children every day, and taught the alphabet again and again. Melody hated it.

paragraphs.context: Then my tornado explosion took over. I flailed and
paragraphs.simple: Melody could not stand it any longer and had one of her fits. She kicked and screamed until she tipped to one side.

paragraphs.context: “School started in August. You haven’t gotten past the
paragraphs.simple: Mom is shocked that after six months the class has not gone past the letter B. She is getting angry.

paragraphs.context: “Well, I think that’s what happened to Melody. She
paragraphs.simple: Mom says Melody screamed because she was bored of doing the same letters again and again. Mom does not blame her.

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Billups quit her job after spring break, so
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Billups left her job after spring break. Melody thinks she expected teaching "dumb" kids to be easy.

paragraphs.context: At least I got to go outside and to
paragraphs.simple: Melody felt sorry for Ollie. At least she could go outside; he only swam in a circle all day and night.

paragraphs.context: But suddenly, for no reason I could figure, Ollie
paragraphs.simple: One day Ollie suddenly jumped out of his bowl and landed on the table, gasping for air.

paragraphs.context: I didn’t know what to do. He’d die without
paragraphs.simple: Melody knew Ollie would die without water, so she screamed for Mom. Mom did not come.

paragraphs.context: I howled once more, but Mom didn’t come running
paragraphs.simple: Melody reached for the bowl to pour water on Ollie, but she knocked the whole bowl over.

paragraphs.context: And I kept wailing. Finally, I heard my mother
paragraphs.simple: Mom finally came and thought Melody had knocked over the bowl on purpose.

paragraphs.context: I wondered if maybe Ollie wasn’t so happy after
paragraphs.simple: Melody wonders if Ollie was tired of his small, boring life. She sometimes feels the same way.

paragraphs.context: There was no way I could explain to Mom
paragraphs.simple: Melody could not tell Mom she had tried to save Ollie. She was angry and sad, and hid her tears.

paragraphs.context: It was a long time before I was ready
paragraphs.simple: For her eighth birthday Dad brought home a big box. Out came a golden puppy.

paragraphs.context: I was the one who named her. Mom and
paragraphs.simple: Melody named the dog by pointing at her favorite candy, butterscotch, because the dog was the same golden color.

paragraphs.context: I was watching something I’d seen a million times
paragraphs.simple: Melody was watching The Wizard of Oz, a movie she knows by heart.

background.note: A famous 1939 movie. A girl named Dorothy travels to the land of Oz with a Scarecrow, a Tin Man and a Cowardly Lion. Each one hopes the Wizard will give him something he is missing.

paragraphs.context: Even though I knew it was coming, when the
paragraphs.simple: Melody laughed so hard at the Tin Man's dance that she fell out of her wheelchair onto the floor.

paragraphs.context: But Butterscotch went to the closed door and scratched
paragraphs.simple: Mom was asleep. Butterscotch scratched at the door and barked louder and louder until Mom came.

paragraphs.context: So what would I ask for? I’d like to
paragraphs.simple: If Melody could ask the Wizard for something, she would ask to sing like the Lion and dance like the Tin Man.

paragraphs.context: I don’t think I’d gained any weight. It was
paragraphs.simple: Mom was tired, sick and throwing up. Melody soon learned that Mom was going to have a baby.

paragraphs.context: She looked me right in the eye. “We’re gonna
paragraphs.simple: Mom says they love Melody as she is, but they hope the new baby will not have the same problems.
hardWords: looked me right in the eye

paragraphs.context: “No! I’m the mother!” she wailed. “It was my
paragraphs.simple: Mom cries that it was her fault Melody was born with problems. Dad tells her it is not her fault.

paragraphs.context: But Penny was born perfect and copper-bright, just
paragraphs.simple: Penny was born healthy, "perfect and copper-bright" like a new penny, and she was a happy baby.

paragraphs.context: It would get quiet once more, but even so
paragraphs.simple: Melody hears her parents argue when they are tired. She feels a bit guilty, thinking life would be easier with only one child, "one with working parts".

paragraphs.context: I once got one of those electronic dolls for
paragraphs.simple: Melody compares herself to an electronic doll with a broken arm that could only do one thing.

paragraphs.context: But Penny! Penny really was a perfect baby. After
paragraphs.simple: Penny learned to sit, roll over and crawl right on time. Everything seemed so easy for her.

paragraphs.context: Dad and his camcorder followed Penny around like the
paragraphs.simple: Dad films everything Penny does. Melody admits she sometimes got tired of watching all the videos.

paragraphs.context: How did her little brain know how to tell
paragraphs.simple: Melody wonders how Penny's brain tells her body what to do. Penny never lies stuck on the floor like Melody did.

paragraphs.context: I think Penny’s third word was “Dee-Dee.” She
paragraphs.simple: One of Penny's first words was "Dee-Dee", her name for Melody. Penny loves to kiss her sister.

paragraphs.context: Drinking stuff is hard for me too. I can’t
paragraphs.simple: Melody cannot hold a cup or use a straw. If someone pours too much, she chokes and makes a mess.

paragraphs.context: Penny wakes every morning asking for her “Doodle,” a
paragraphs.simple: Penny carries her old stuffed toy, Doodle, everywhere. Nobody knows what animal it is.

paragraphs.context: Even though the doctors said it would be impossible
paragraphs.simple: The doctors said it was impossible, but by age three Melody had found a way to show Mom when she needed the toilet.

paragraphs.context: Mom and I can sometimes talk without words. I
paragraphs.simple: Mom and Melody can often understand each other without words. When Melody points, Mom usually knows what she means.

paragraphs.context: Mom knows when I’m hungry or thirsty, and whether
paragraphs.simple: Mom can tell if Melody is hungry, thirsty, really sick, or just pretending to be sick to stay home.

paragraphs.context: For my tenth birthday I got a whole book
paragraphs.simple: Melody loves Garfield cartoons. Garfield the cat cannot talk, but his thoughts are written in bubbles above his head.

background.note: A famous comic strip about a lazy, funny orange cat. In the comic, Garfield's thoughts appear in "thought bubbles" over his head.

paragraphs.context: But sometimes that’s how I feel—like wouldn’t it
paragraphs.simple: Melody wishes her thoughts could appear in bubbles over her head, so people would know what she thinks.

paragraphs.context: When I try to talk, the words are exploding
paragraphs.simple: Words explode in Melody's brain, but when she tries to talk, only squeaks and sounds come out.

paragraphs.context: For example, one afternoon earlier this summer, I had
paragraphs.simple: Melody wants a Big Mac, but her board has only a few words. Dad tries hard and asks many yes-or-no questions, but he cannot guess.

paragraphs.context: I shouted, “Uh!” as loud as I could, and
paragraphs.simple: Weeks later Dad stopped at McDonald's by chance. He never understood her first request, but Melody was happy anyway.

paragraphs.context: Fifth grade started a few weeks ago, and a
paragraphs.simple: Melody gets an electric wheelchair, and the school starts "inclusion" classes.

background.note: Putting students with disabilities in regular classes with other students for some or all of the day, instead of keeping them in a separate room.

paragraphs.context: For me, it’s all about the freedom. Now I
paragraphs.simple: With her electric chair Melody can move by herself. She does not have to wait for help.

paragraphs.context: She told us on the first day, “I’m gonna
paragraphs.simple: The new teacher, Mrs. Shannon, has a Southern accent. She promises to work very hard to help the class learn and grow.

paragraphs.simple: Mom has a headache and wishes she could go back to bed. She is supposed to be off today.

paragraphs.simple: Melody screams and kicks wildly to warn Mom. Mom thinks she is having a fit.

paragraphs.simple: Mom screams. Police, a fire truck and an ambulance come.

paragraphs.simple: After the ambulance leaves, Mrs. V puts Melody in her chair and gives her Penny's wet, dirty Doodle.

paragraphs.simple: Melody types that she wants to be like other kids.

paragraphs.simple: The phone call comes: Penny has internal injuries and a broken leg, but she survived surgery.

paragraphs.simple: Connor gives Melody the small ninth-place trophy, to make up for leaving her.

paragraphs.simple: The trophy is cheap plastic, and the school's name is spelled wrong.

paragraphs.simple: Melody laughs and laughs. The trophy falls and breaks.

paragraphs.simple: Melody says fifth grade is hard for every kid: homework, clothes, parents and wanting to be cool.

paragraphs.simple: Melody has the same worries as other kids, plus many more. Maybe she is not so different after all.

paragraphs.simple: Melody compares her life to a puzzle without the picture on the box. She does not know how it will turn out.

paragraphs.simple: Penny is home from the hospital with a cast and a new red hat. Everyone spoils her.

paragraphs.simple: Melody starts her autobiography on Elvira. She has a lot to say and "just one thumb" to say it with. The book's first chapter follows.

paragraphs.context: Giddy up oom poppa oom poppa mow mow
paragraphs.mainIdea: This line is from the song Elvira. The sounds are not a normal sentence.
paragraphs.simple: Melody is remembering a country song. Giddy up is what you call to a horse to make it go. The oom-poppa sounds are the beat of the song, not words she is saying to someone.

paragraphs.context: The choir at church: Hallelujah, hallelujah, amen.
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is a short bit of a church song.
paragraphs.simple: Melody remembers the church choir singing. Hallelujah and amen are song words of praise. She is listing words she has heard, not starting a new story.

paragraphs.context: Daddy brought you a play-pretty
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mom calls the toy a play-pretty. That is not a real word.
paragraphs.simple: Mom uses a baby voice and says Dad brought a play-pretty. She made that word up. It only means a toy to play with. Melody has to guess, because nobody explains it in this line.

paragraphs.context: Big old Nimbus up there—he’s black and powerful
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. V makes the rain clouds into people in a little story.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V points at a dark cloud and names him Nimbus. She says he wants to marry a soft cloud called Miss Cumulus, and he makes storms when he is angry. She is playing with the weather, not telling a true story about two people.

paragraphs.context: They call him “Dimwit Dimming” behind his back.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The students give Mr. Dimming a mean nickname that twists his name.
paragraphs.simple: Many students do not like the history teacher. Behind his back they call him Dimwit Dimming. A dimwit is a foolish person. The nickname sounds like his real name, Dimming. Melody thinks it is unkind, because he is actually smart.

paragraphs.context: the guy who invented the flush toilet was named Thomas Crapper
paragraphs.mainIdea: Connor wants the report because the inventor's name sounds like a bathroom joke.
paragraphs.simple: Connor asks to write about Thomas Crapper, the man he thinks invented the flush toilet. The class laughs because the last name sounds like a rude bathroom word. The joke is the name, not the history.

paragraphs.context: They make computers for the special eddies?
paragraphs.mainIdea: A student makes a rude joke on the words special ed.
paragraphs.simple: Someone sees Melody's speaking computer and asks if they make computers for the special eddies. Special ed is short for special education. The speaker turns ed into eddies, as if the students were a funny kind of thing. It is mean, and it is not a real group of people.

paragraphs.context: Happy, happy, happy, clap your feet
paragraphs.mainIdea: Penny is singing a made-up baby song, not giving orders.
paragraphs.simple: Penny sings a silly song: happy, happy, happy, clap your feet. The lines rhyme and jump. She is playing. She does not really want Melody to clap her feet.

sentences.context: Words have always swirled around me like snowflakes—each one delicate and different, each one melting untouched in my hands.
sentences.simple: Words have always been all around Melody, like falling snow. Each word is special, but she can never catch and use one.
sentences.main: Words are near her but out of reach.

parts.text: Words have always swirled around me
parts.meaning: Words have always moved around me
every word is fine and special,

parts.text: each one melting untouched in my hands.
parts.meaning: and every word disappears before I can use it.

sentences.grammar: "Like + noun" compares two things. "Each one + -ing" adds a picture of every single word.

sentences.context: I can almost hear colors and smell images when music is played.
sentences.simple: When Melody hears music, she seems to see colors and smell pictures.
sentences.grammar: "Almost" makes it softer: it is nearly true. "Is played" is passive: someone plays the music.

sentences.context: It’s like I have a camera in my head, and if I see or hear something, I click it, and it stays.

parts.meaning: My mind works like a camera,

parts.text: and if I see or hear something,
parts.meaning: and when I see or hear anything,
I take a picture of it,

sentences.grammar: "It's like..." = it is similar to... "If" gives a condition; the next parts say what happens.

sentences.simple: A person is much more than the name of an illness written in a doctor's notes.

parts.text: But a person is so much more
than the name of a diagnosis on a chart!
parts.meaning: than the name of her medical problem in a file!

sentences.grammar: "So much more than" = far greater than. A "diagnosis" is the doctor's name for an illness.

parts.meaning: I feel I am in a cage

parts.text: with no door and no key.

sentences.grammar: "It's like" introduces a comparison. "With no..." describes the cage.

parts.meaning: is a bit like a coat

parts.text: with the buttons done up in the wrong holes.
parts.meaning: that is buttoned in the wrong places.

sentences.grammar: "Sort of like" = a bit like. "Done up" = fastened (buttons).

parts.meaning: of the same bowl, log and circle every day.

parts.meaning: I feel like the famous explorer

sentences.simple: How your body looks does not show how smart you are.
sentences.grammar: "What ... looks like" is a whole clause used as the subject. "Have nothing to do with" = not be connected to.

sentences.context: To people like Claire and Molly, I say, “We all have disabilities. What’s yours?”

parts.text: To people like Claire and Molly,

sentences.context: Words float out of lips that say nice things to me, but eyes tell the truth.

parts.text: that say nice things to me,
parts.meaning: and say kind things to me,
but their eyes show their true feelings.

sentences.grammar: "But" shows a contrast between what people say and what they feel.

sentences.context: Never had I wanted words more.
sentences.simple: Melody had never wanted to be able to speak as much as at this moment.
sentences.grammar: When a sentence starts with "Never", the verb comes before the subject: "Never had I..." = "I had never...". This makes it stronger.

sentences.context: People love you because you’re Melody, not because of what you can or cannot do.

parts.meaning: not because of your skills or problems.

sentences.grammar: "Because + clause" and "because of + noun" both give reasons. "Not because of" says what is NOT the reason.

sentences.grammar: "Something to + verb" = something that needs that action. "To say it with" = to use for saying it.

sentences.context: Well, I never!” Mrs. Billups countered.
